UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST EXPORTATION OF CANADIAN POTATOES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past year the United States Department of Commerce, through its agencies, has been investigating the nature of trade in potatoes between Canada and the United States. It found that there was some reason to consider that there was both dumping and damage in shipments to the United States.
I submit that there was probably evidence under the letter of the law to substantiate those findings. 1 also submit to you that the traditional commodity trade between Canada and the United States has been going on nearly a century, and the nature of the business concerned was not taken into consideration as the letter of the law was applied.
I think it is imperative that all Ministers of the Crown who may be interested in agriculture or international trade should make the strongest possible representations to their counterparts in the United States, because this will be a benchmark decision. While it only relates to potatoes, it opens the door for comparable applications for consideration of dumping or damage under United States law by other commodity groups in the United States. It also gives Canada an opportunity to interfere with imports of horticultural products from the United States.
Any final decision by the ITC, which I understand would be reached on November 18, could be very detrimental to our historic trade practices-

speechtext:

subsubtopic: WAGES OWED MAISLIN COMPANY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Twelve months after receiving an emergency $34 million loan guarantee from the federal Government, Montreal-based Maislin Industries Limited is on the verge of bankruptcy. Apparently the company has run out of money for its operations. The company has laid off all but a few of its 3,500 employees and now Alan Maislin, the company vice-chairman and former president, has resigned and is supporting the employees in their fight to get moneys owed to them in back pay.
Secured creditors are owed $59.4 million. The Canadian-Imperial Bank of Commerce moved to protect its $38.8 million interest by calling the loan. The National Bank of Canada is owed nearly $7 million. The unsecured creditors are owed $18.3 million.
In Quebec and Ontario outraged employees of the main domestic subsidiary, Maislin Transport Limited, form picket lines. One Montreal group has learned that its pay cheques will not be honoured.
Surely laid-off workers should have first priority over secured creditors and unsecured creditors. The financial security of workers who have lost their jobs and are owed back wages should be our first concern. If we are unable to secure full payment of back wages we should try to ensure that at least a partial payment of up to one month's wages will be issued to all workers who have entitlement.
Perhaps the Government can help ensure that priority be given to these workers and, if necessary, legislation should be passed to provide workers with at least up to one month's back wages and allowances ahead of all other creditors-

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA PEACE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House that the foreign ministers of nine Latin American countries have agreed on a plan for peace in Central America, calling for regional negotiations, disarmament, and a cutback in foreign advisers.
The four Contadoran countries, Columbia, Mexico, Panama, and Venezuela, have made peace proposals before, but this is the first time that the foreign ministers of Guatemala, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Honduras have endorsed such a plan.
Details of the framework agreement are not known yet but the main objectives are the following: first, immediate and progressive disarmament after an inventory of armaments in the region; second, a reduction in the number of foreign military advisers; and third, a permanent dialogue between governments and their internal opposition movements to lead to precise electoral processes.
The Contadora group stresses the efforts to bring Central American conflicts to the negotiating table and eventually to use ballots instead of bullets to settle differences. At this time the document has gone to the governments of nine countries for approval.
The group is calling for foreign governments to refrain from military intervention and to co-operate by carrying out concrete actions of assistance. In this light I call upon the Government of Canada to support formally, in a much more obvious way, the efforts of the Contadora group and, through every diplomatic force available, to push for the withdrawal of all foreign forces from the area.

subtopic: GARNISHEE, ATTACHMENT AND PENSION DIVERSION ACT DELAY IN PROCLAMATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, litigation involving this legislation is presently in the courts. As Hon. Members may know, there is a dispute between the Department of Justice and the House of Commons as to whether Members and employees of the House of Commons are affected by that legislation. That has had consequences for the general proclamation of the legislation. There is a case now in the courts on which I cannot comment, but I hope that the matter will be resolved shortly by the courts, if not in some other fashion. It may be that we ought to seek further legislative clarification on this. I might consult the House Leader and my Opposition critic in the next week or two to see whether we can arrive at a legislative clarification so that this spectacle, which might be considered rather unedifying by the people of the country, would not continue to be dragged on.

Mr. Speaker, given the fact that the Bill was passed in some parts unanimously and that, to some degree, there was unanimity throughout its entire passage, could the Minister of Justice explain whether it is Members of the House or Senators who are objecting to the proclamation of the Bill, or does it come from officers of the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there may or may not be Members who are taking positions on this; I am not aware of that. The primary difficulty is that officials of the House, 1 think acting in pursuance of the tradition of parliamentary immunity from various kinds of legislation, have taken the position that Members of parliament and employees of Parliament should not be touched. I would not like to say that this is not a matter of importance. The point precisely is that I think Members had one intention when the legislation was passed. It is now running into these difficulties, which 1 quite agree with the Hon. Member have to be clarified within the next few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. It is a question which may well be directed to the Minister of Trade, but I believe it is the Minister of National Revenue who handles it. How can we possibly effect the kind of economic recovery in Canada about which everyone speaks as being necessary, when the Anti-Dumping Tribunal and the anti-dumping legislation are totally inadequate, when the steel industry is already being subjected to tremendous pressures from dumping from at least 12 other countries in the world, and when the result of this dumping is an increase in unemployment and a decrease in productivity? When will we get some adequate legislation to protect our manufacturers from the totally inadequate legislation which currently exists?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member ought to know that responsibility for our antidumping policy legislation lies with the Minister of Finance. He should also remember that during the past two years, the Government has been considering a number of changes in our anti-dumping legislation, and thirdly, the Department of National Revenue regularly responds to requests for anti-dumping investigations from various sectors of the Canadian economy, including the steel industry, the heavy equipment sector, and so on. We carry out the investigations as quickly as possible, preliminary analyses are made fairly regularly, and we try to be as effective as we can.

subtopic: ACTION BY STATE OF FLORIDA AGAINST CANADIAN CITIZEN
ACTION BY STATE OF FLORIDA AGAINST CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and is prompted by news reports from this morning and yesterday concerning the decision made by the State of Florida to re-lay charges against Sidney Jaffe and that, in the event that his application for parole is successful, he will be re-arrested. This whole affair, beginning with the abduction of Mr. Jaffe, has cast very serious questions upon the quality of justice administered in that State and the fairness of the judgment of the Attorney General of that State. Accordingly, 1 would ask the Prime Minister what the country of Canada is prepared to do in terms of retaliatory action against conduct which is so unacceptable to us?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACTION BY STATE OF FLORIDA AGAINST CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is quite right when he states that the conduct at the basis of the Jaffe case is completely unacceptable, not only to Canada but to other civilized nations. We have taken the strongest possible exception to that action and I have attended many meetings devoted to this purpose, including quite a number of meetings with American officials.
The case is still in the legal process in the United States. The Government of Canada has commenced a legal action for habeas corpus in the Federal Court of that country and 1 believe that we must see through to the end the legal process which we have begun. Mr. Jaffe has the right to his own forms of legal process. His goals are not precisely the same as ours, although obviously his goals and our goals do overlap considerably.
1 believe that it is very important, Mr. Speaker, because we are taking a stand based upon legality and upon civilized life, that we follow all of the legalities in this case ourselves.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is again directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The major oil companies have moved the price of gasoline up 15 cents per litre. One cent per litre is worth $250 million to oil companies-

speechtext: Would the Hon. Member please state his question?

speechtext:

Hon. Judy Erola (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I have attempted twice to answer the Hon. Member's question, and I shall try for the third time. 1 believe that it is fair to comment that much of this increase is due to increases in taxes which are, of course, at the provincial level. Let me make it very clear that this is also part of the problem.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Justice and concerns the same subject. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA-UNITED STATES EXTRADITION TREATY BE SUSPENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
1 certainly share the feelings of frustration that the Hon. Member has expressed with the State of Florida. I do not think that the proper reaction at this stage would be to follow the course of action that my hon. friend recommends. 1 believe that we have no alternative at the moment but to place our emphasis and to put our priorities on the legal process because, after all, the legal process is what has been departed from by those who have seized Jaffe and put him in prison in Florida.

subsubtopic: INVOCATION OF DIPLOMATIC IMMUNITY
speechtext:
1.	Was diplomatic immunity invoked by countries to avoid prosecution for alleged violations of Canadian law, including traffic violations, in (a) 1981 (b) 1982 and, if so, on how many occasions for each country?
2.	What was the nature of each offence and in which municipality did the alleged infraction occur?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INVOCATION OF DIPLOMATIC IMMUNITY
speechtext:
1. (a) In 1981, 38 Diplomatic Missions requested the cancellation of 169 traffic violations and five Missions invoked diplomatic immunity for five other offences.
(b)	In 1982, 39 Diplomatic Missions requested the cancellation of 240 traffic violations and six Missions invoked diplomatic immunity on six occasions for other offences.
2.	The 169 traffic violations cancelled in 1981 included parking violations (132), speeding (28) suspension of a driver's licence (4), impaired driving (3) and failure to wear a seat belt (2). The other offences of 1981 consisted in shop-lifting (3), fraudulent use of a cheque (1) and illegal use of the mail (1). The traffic violations occured in the Ottawa/Hull area (146), in the Montreal area (15), in other parts of Ontario (7) and Alberta (1). The five other offences took place in the Ottawa/ Hull area.
The 240 traffic violations cancelled in 1982 consisted of parking infractions (220), speeding (14), failure to wear a seat belt (4), impaired driving (1) and the use of studded tires (1). They occured in the Ottawa/Hull area (217), in the Montreal area (15), in the Toronto area (5), and in Vancouver (3). The other offenses consisted in shop-lifting (4), fraudulent use of a cheque (I) and possession of a small quantity of marijuana (1). Five of the latter offences took place in the Ottawa/Hull area and one in Montreal.
The Department considers that disclosure of the names of the Missions concerned would not be in keeping with Canada's obligation under Article 22 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations requesting the host country to take all appropriate steps to protect Missions from disturbance of their peace or impairment of their rights.
September 16, 1983

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased with this opportunity today to make a few comments on the readjustment of electoral boundaries. On February 17 of this year, I appeared before the Commissioners to submit objections concerning my constituency of Verdun-Saint Paul, which I have represented in the House since 1977.
I drew their attention to some minor changes regarding my constituency. My purpose was to draw their attention to these changes that would enable me to maintain proper representation of this constituency in Parliament. I feel the changes are in accordance with the Elections Act, and I earnestly hope that the Commissioners will endorse my recommendations and so keep parishes and communities intact.
The changes I am proposing are aimed solely at maintaining the natural identity of the constituency, and as such, they also meet the population requirements as defined by the Commission. After several meetings with my constituents, I was told by everyone that the Commission definitely had to respect the wishes of the people.
At the meeting on February 17 of this year, a number of Members concerned by the adjustments appeared before the Commission to support these recommendations and provide additional information.
Mr. Speaker, today, I would like to talk about the history of my constituency. The town of Verdun is more than a hundred years old. When the history of Montreal was written, the author may not have had much to say about the history of this very small piece of land. The fact is, that although the land was parcelled out some time ago, it was not developed until much later. Until the beginning of this century, the town of Verdun was a swamp flooded by the St. Lawrence for most of the year.
The present town occupies a narrow strip between the St. Lawrence and the Lachine Canal, and it was not until 1852 that the town began to take shape. Nowadays, Verdun has a very high population density, although there has always been a ban on buildings over three stories high. Only lle-des-Sceurs
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act has allowed the construction of modern apartment highrises during the last few years. Within a period of 100 years, Verdun's population has grown from its initial 200 inhabitants to its present number of 80,000, a case that may be unique.
Like all towns, the population of Verdun is made up of members of the working class, led by a middle class elite relatively speaking-a small aristocracy of upstanding citizens. Today, Verdun has made a name for itself in more than one field, but on the whole, its leaders have been content with modest aspirations. As the town developed, it always kept its identity as a parish. If we are to understand the significance of such statements, I think it is essential to recognize that the attitudes, traditions and habits of communities that develop in an urban environment are fundamentally different from those in rural centres.
It is common knowledge that in smaller centres, there is a trend towards movements, groups and associations that tend to attract people with common interests. This very typical tendency is often due to a very definite desire and motivation to acquire the mechanisms, institutions, tools and means to renew, in some cases, and to improve and develop in others, the community's social, cultural, economic, athletic and other resources. Verdun has 21 churches, including 7 Catholic churches and 14 Protestant churches, the latter representing 7 denominations. Over the years, a school administration has developed with components representing communities that have worked together and developed in the same environment in the course of time.
Economically speaking, Verdun was able to develop its territory by taking advantage of the land available on lle-des-Soeurs and bringing in service industries which provided jobs for local people. The entire community always has direct access to its federal Member of Parliament and the Commission should realize that it must respect the identity of this community and refrain from further enlarging its territory, bearing in mind that part of the territory of Montreal, namely Cote-St. Paul and Ville-Emard, is already part of this federal constituency.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I earnestly hope that constituencies that have objections will be allowed to ask for a new adjustment before the changes proposed by the Commission are accepted, so that we can have a chance to submit the views of our constituents.

Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act Hon. Judy Erola (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs): Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the convenience of being able to present my objections this afternoon and I thank Hon. Members of the House for their kindness.
1 rise today on a matter of supreme importance to my constituents. I might add that I had promised them that today was going to be the day I raised these objections, and they are most keen to hear them.
I might add as well that 1 am doing what ! think is the most important thing a Member of Parliament is elected to do, and that is to protect and fight for the people we represent.
There are few more solemn bonds in our national institutions than those between the electors and the elected. To the elected official, the people in the communities he or she represents are not numbers on a StatsCan ledger, or social insurance or telephone numbers. They are not a faceless collection of nondescript human ciphers. Our constituents are the women, men and children we meet in our offices, on the street, in the schools, stores and businesses, at the untold number of meetings and social gatherings we attend. They are real people with real concerns, opinions, and attitudes. They have something to say and it is my job to listen and bring their concerns to the House. We must see that whatever subsequent action that may be required is taken to make government represent fully their interests and satisfy their wishes.
It is true that the women and men elected to represent a constituency by necessity assume a sense of geographic parochialism. In most cases it is a sense of home and family. One does not arbitrarily toss a dart at an electoral map and declare an intention to run for office and then pretend to truly represent the people residing therein. We are elected not because we hope to descend from on high and offer our services to the people we hope to represent. No, Mr. Speaker, we must be totally a part of the people, chosen through their collective wisdom as the person they feel most comfortable with as their voice in the larger institution of government.
Consequently, a Member of Parliament regards the people of his or her riding with not only respect, a sense of service and a desire to better their lives, but with a certain reverence much akin to the sanctity of the family. Each and every person who resides in my riding is important to me, no matter what his or her political affiliation, regardless of whatever disagreements there may be with my particular views on any number of issues. Let me assure you that they let me know! As in any family, differences exist, but the bond of commonality, of shared interests and experiences, transcend the strains which may occur from time to time.
So, Mr. Speaker, I stand here today in this chamber, so distant in geography and daily experience from the people of Nickel Belt, to come to the defence of communities in my riding which threaten to be orphaned-literally orphaned-by the electoral distribution process.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, 1 never thought I would find myself forced to justify to the higher powers the inclusion, the continued membership in the Nickel Belt family, of the Town

speechtext:
Come aboard! We would love to have you but there are no fish there, unfortunately.
St. Charles, Mr. Speaker, has been placed in what can only be described as a totally ludicrous situation. On one side of the street a person who needs to contact his or her federal representative would, as is now the case, come to my office in Sudbury, while his neighbour on the other side of the street would have to go to Kirkland Lake, a locality, pleasant as it is, as different in makeup as Calgary is to Sudbury.
What I find most surprising, and I must say disturbing, Mr. Speaker, is that in the original redistribution proposal, Nickel Belt was threatened with the loss of the town of Onaping Falls. We dealt with that through proper channels. This community is not only bonded to the Nickel basin communities by reason of geography and commerce, but is actually a member of the regional municipality of Sudbury.
This proposal to lop off a limb of the Sudbury tree was vigorously and vehemently opposed by me and hundreds of concerned parties from the entire region. We made our representations very forcefully and I am pleased to see an obvious absurdity has been corrected. However, you can imagine my surprise when the changes were unfolded and I was faced with an identical situation by the proposal to take the Town of Nickel Centre to a patently unnatural electoral family.
Nickel Centre, like Onaping Falls, is also a member of the regional government, with all the attendant interlocking services which governments of a region offer. While Nickel Centre, I might add, takes pride in its individual character, it is nevertheless an integral component of the regional municipality with its focus being the City of Sudbury. It looks to the Sudbury population centre for its commercial interests, its transportation needs, its media coverage and information systems.
To suggest that the people of Nickel Centre should or could cut themselves out of the Sudbury basin orbit and then develop an arbitrary affiliation with the riding of Timiskaming, with its nucleus in Kirkland Lake, is really quite silly to the residents of the area. It would be laughable if it were not such an affront to the years of traditional association these citizens cherish with their fellow citizens in the other Sudbury basin communities.
1 am quite sure that the designers of this anomaly could not have done so deliberately, having an awareness of the on the street impact which such a change would create. I point now to another town, that of St. Charles.

As far as St. Charles is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I must say that a community divided is a sad sight to see. As I pointed out earlier, this proposal means that this community and its neighbours, in a relatively isolated area, will be divided in two and forced to seek political representation in two geographically separated areas, namely Kirkland Lake and Sudbury. In addition to the inconvience to residents in the eastern part of the village, the entire community is affected by this confusing situation.

While this suggested alteration may have been made in a well meaning way, I urge the commission to look more closely at its implications and to restore the cloven Town of St. Charles in its original fullness and vitality to the Nickel Belt constituency.
A point 1 must make, Mr. Speaker, in this discussion, and the reason I am here today defending my constituents on the more vulnerable outer flanks of Nickel Belt, is that there is an apparent disproportionate allocation of population among northern Ontario ridings. The reason Nickel Belt has been nibbled at in various redistribution schemes-and I might add this is not the first crack-is that my riding has the largest population base of the northern Ontario ridings, and Timiskaming to the northeast has the least. Consequently, when the commission went shopping for more electors, it was obvious that I was the prime candidate.
I suggest to the commission, Mr. Speaker, that the allegedly inadequate population base in Timiskaming, which has prompted the quest for electors, is a skewed and inaccurate picture of the current population figures in my neighbouring riding of Timiskaming. It is my honestly held belief, and I feel this belief is shared also by the current sitting Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall), that the 1981 census was taken at a time of abnormally low population levels, in a territory which is cyclically prone to fluctuation due to the boom and bust of the mining cycle in that area.
I will argue that the population today is substantially greater than it was at the time of the census, and I will go even further to suggest that before the next election or the implementation of redistribution, whichever comes first, I know that the measures of this Government to maintain and expand the industrial, commercial and agricultural base of Timiskaming will continue to bear results, and Timiskaming's population will increase accordingly.
I would add, Mr. Speaker, that while one may expect the most populous riding to be picked on when it comes to justifying the continued existence of a riding, or creating a new riding configuration, the population figures of my riding do not exceed by a remarkable amount those proscribed by law. I will be very specific. The Electoral Boundaries Readjustment
September 16, 1983

Act stipulates that the electoral quota for the riding should be 82,143. However, if one considers that the Act permits a variance of 25 per cent plus or minus that figure to an upward maximum at 102,679 and a low of 61,607 Nickel Belt at 85,000 fits quite comfortably in the middle and very much within the guidelines.
However, the damage inflicted on the cohesion of my riding by the random search for numbers-and I say "random", mere numbers-far outweighs any cosmetic, statistical advantage gained in shoring up the figures of less densely populated ridings. If the goal is to preserve 11 or 12 northern Ontario ridings, I firmly believe more logical and less disruptive alternatives exist.
In making the case for preservation of portions of my riding which are threatened by redistribution, 1 have the added confidence of knowing that there is virtually unanimous local opposition to the proposed changes. I would say that the reaction to the boundary changes contradicts and refutes the conclusion of a recent Gallup survey that Canadians believe their Parliament is irrelevant. The response to the redistribution proposals has been overwhelmingly negative and, I might add, very emotional, indicating to me that the people's attachment to their riding runs deep and has a very personal significance.
Let me put on record just a few of the comments 1 have received. First, from the Township of Ratter & Dunnet, I quote:
It would create a great hardship for the voters to have to adjust to such drastic changes. The Timiskaming constituency office is located in Kirkland Lake, this being some 200 miles away from Warren, making it practically impossible for residents to meet with their MP.
From Phil Bonhomme, councillor of the Town of Nickel Centre, 1 quote:
Logic dictates that radical shifts create chaos, additional costs and leave the public in a state of frustration.
From the Corporation of the Township of Casimir, Jennings and Appleby, I quote:
1 am sure you can appreciate the effect it would have on our small community to have our town cut in half by this decision to use the Highway 535 to determine the boundary of these ridings.
From the Regional Development Corporation of Sudbury, I quote:
It is our strong belief that if the Regional Municipality of Sudbury is to continue to strive for economic diversification, it must do so as a strong and united force, especially in its dealings with the senior levels of government. To lose the Town of Nickel Centre to the Timiskaming riding would result in a fragmentation of this united front, thereby creating a negative impact on the region's economic development aspirations.
From a brief submitted by the Town of Nickel Centre, 1 quote:
The entire Sudbury regional community is astonished by the commission's decision. There has been no advance notification of the commission's intention to remove the town from the Nickel Belt riding, nor was there an opportunity for a public hearing on this latest proposal. There is a deep feeling that the community's interests, both present and traditional, affecting the Town of Nickel Centre, have not been respected.

Member has outlined today, there has been a general acceptance by other Members in northern Ontario that the final maps prepared dealt generally very well with the representations and suggestions made at the hearings last January in Sudbury and Ottawa. Indeed, the Commission, I think, did an admirable job in establishing an average population for the 11 seats in northern Ontario at 70,993 people, whereas in southern Ontario it was about 15 per cent more, or 83,449 electors per constituency based on the 1981 census. That takes into account the vast size of the constituencies, the difficulty of drawing lines and getting a reasonable balance of size and community of interests, and the possibility of the Members serving those constituencies after they are elected. For example in my own constituency they recommended that a large portion of the area north of Sault Ste. Marie be put in with the Kapuskasing-Cochrane-Superior riding, and indeed they responded to those representations, 1 think, in a very good way.
I believe the vast majority of Members in the north are quite satisfied with the redistribution, with the exception of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt. 1 am sure the representations that she has made here this afternoon so effectively will be taken into account by the Commissioners in their final proclamation of the electoral boundaries. I think it is important that Members not only say when there are objections but also when things are right, because sometimes boundaries tend to be changed if nobody stands up and says what is right about the redistribution.
There are a couple of small, technical objections which I would like to make concerning the Algoma riding. 1 am generally very happy with the redistribution which has taken place, mostly because it represents a continuation of the existing boundaries and it is very confusing for people who are not very conscious of political boundaries to have those
changed every ten years. Of course, they are not only changed federally but provincially.
There are a couple of small, technical suggestions I would like to make to the Commission in drafting their final boundaries, and one is the Carscaden poll which is located immediately adjacent to the Town of Onaping Falls in the Nickel Belt riding. 1 ask that it be located within the Nickel Belt riding because of the community of interests, the geography and the general means of transportation between those areas.
Likewise, in the City of Sault Ste. Marie, at the opposite end of my constituency towards the West, in the drawing of the boundaries between the Algoma constituency and the City of Sault Ste. Marie constituency, I think it would really simplify matters a great deal if they were to run the boundary line between the two constituencies along People's Road from the second line to the city boundaries just to make it more simple and easy for people to remember where the boundary is and to easily identify it. I would like to see those two small amendments taken into account by the Commission in their final boundary determination.
I think the process has worked fairly well this time. It has been generally responsive to most of the ten Members in the north, if not to the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt. But I am sure they will be considering her objections.
I think we as Members recognize that when you are dealing with 88 per cent of the land mass of the Province of Ontario and trying to carve up northern Ontario into 11 constituencies, it is a difficult task to bring together a community of interests to a manageable size and to take into account transportation routes and systems, media systems, distribution of information and all the rest of it. Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be a brief one but it does arise from the concerns expressed to the House by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mrs. Erola). If the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the Province of Ontario were to take seriously and answer the grievances presented to the House by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, the vast region of northern Ontario, one of the very important resource regions of this country, could be facing once again the dilemma and agony we faced at the last redistribution, namely the loss of another seat.
Some Hon. Members in the House will remember the last redistribution and the extreme disquiet and dismay that was felt by the Members of Parliament for northern Ontario and the people they represented, not simply on the question that one Member of Parliament might not have a seat and could not continue on. That was not the issue. The issue involved the northern part of the Province of Ontario which, in terms of its land mass, in excess of 50 per cent of the Province, has always
September 16, 1983

felt at a grave disadvantage in seeing that it has its fair share of interest from the national Parliament of this country.
I want very quickly to repeat what the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) said and indicate to the House that 1 think the work done by the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the Province of Ontario, as it applies to the north of the Province of Ontario, was exemplary in every way. It did an outstanding job. It was responsive, sympathetic and understanding. I can just give one example without boring the House with details. There were some suggestions in its first report which my constituents found to be unacceptable. Certain community of interest principles were seriously violated. I, and representatives from these communities made representations in Sudbury. The Commission responded positively and every recommendation that was put forward was accepted, because it was acceptable and it recognized a basic principle that we in northern Ontario all must accept, and that is that if we want to retain our level of representation, there must be a little give and there must be some take.
That is what bothered me so much when 1 listened to the speech of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt. Here we are not speaking of a constituency being picked on. We are not speaking of a constituency being dealt with in some kind of random fashion. We are not speaking of being fiercely protective of our own little constituency in terms of population. What we are speaking of is a region of this country that deserves to be represented in the Parliament of Canada. I suggest that those interests go far beyond whether a community in one corner of one constituency of northern Ontario will be relocated in another. There is a larger issue here, and it is for that reason that I have risen to speak in the debate.
I said that the Electoral Boundaries Commission was responsive in Sudbury, but there were those who made representations in Sudbury along the lines of "Do not in any way touch my constituency; do not alter it in any fashion whatsoever because 1 have become very attached to it, it is mine; it belongs to me and leave it the way it is". 1 found that kind of representation to be reprehensible. I heard it again today and I think it is unacceptable. At the end of those proceedings in Sudbury, I commented to the Commissioners; "if you listened to the arguments that you have heard here today of not touching one constituency that has a rather larger number of persons than other constituencies, if you were to follow that pattern, then northern Ontario would again suffer the loss of a constituency". All of the Commissioners nodded their heads affirmatively and quite vigorously, agreeing that that would be the exact outcome.
There is no comparison between the present Electoral Boundaries Commission for the Province of Ontario and its predecessor which drew up the boundaries with which we had to deal in 1979. This is an enlightened Commission which was responsive, doing an excellent job. The one in 1979 was close-minded, doing severe damage to northern Ontario. We are still suffering from the effects of its decision which was a totally unnecessary one.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
Because it is so directly related, it might now be a good moment to pay a word of tribute to the late Hon. R. K. Andras, who took such a profound and deep interest in the whole region of northern Ontario for which he had responsibility. When the Electoral Boundaries Commission made its unfortunate decision, 1 remember well how the Hon. R. K. Andras, in this very House, drafted a Bill which would have allowed northern Ontario to retain its level of representation. Only in the dying moments of the debate, because there was not enough time allowed, and because we needed unanimous consent and someone would not give it, did we fail. However, I want to pay tribute to a man who not only had a great national constituency and was an outstanding Parliamentarian in terms of representing his own riding, but also one who, when it came to paying attention to his regional responsibilities and doing it in a way which was genuine, coming from the heart, demonstrated that kind of leadership which is difficult to replace. We sadly miss the Hon. Bob Andras in northern Ontario.
I will close by saying again that the Electoral Boundaries Commission for Ontario has done good work. If it listens carefully to what the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt said and it can make some modest changes to meet her demands, that is fine. However, if it must reduce northern Ontario by another seat, then 1 say to the Commissioners: "Reject totally and out of hand the representations made by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt".

Mr. Speaker, when I came to the House of Commons in 1965, I had a small, neat, compact constituency of only 55,000 square miles. After the redistribution that took place in 1969, my constituency expanded to about 75,000 square miles, but the Commission did so by taking the heart of the constituency out so that when I wanted to go from one end of the constituency in a north-south direction to the other, 1 hdd to go through the constituency which was then represented by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior who was then the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay. The next redistribution took my constituency to a size of 155,000 square miles. The proposed redistribution will reduce it to about 150,000 square miles.
The prospect in my constituency has been massive increases in size. The problem is that there has been no one centre in my riding. What I have is a group of small little towns scattered so that there is no one centre one can go into with a view to being able to capture the attention of the bulk of the population.
We have accepted the fact that this constituency has grown with such tremendous force over the last 20 years because the price of doing so has been to allow northern Ontario to maintain more seats than it might otherwise have had under another kind of distribution system. Our dilemma is that our population is marginal from the point of view of holding 11 seats. Furthermore, the population tends to be concentrated in particular areas, leaving vast areas with relatively small populations.

September 16, 1983
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
What we have come down to is the classical trauma of northwestern Ontario in a redistribution period. The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) mentioned the last redistribution. It was very traumatic for us because it cost us a seat in northern Ontario, reducing our representation. 1 think that in terms of regions the size of ours, we were about the only region in Canada to lose seats. It meant an enormous shuffling around of constituency boundaries and it caused enormous difficulty to constituents in finding out to whom they were to go. It also made it very difficult for Members of Parliament to discharge their customary duties.
We now have a situation where the redistribution that has come about has been accepted, by and large. We recognized from the beginning, when the process started, that we would have to accept distortions in the representation in order to be able to maintain 11 seats in northern Ontario. 1 recognize, representing the largest seat in terms of area in northern Ontario and also one of the highest average populations in northern Ontario, that I would not obtain relief from the kind of geographical expansion that has taken place. Other Members accepted the fact that they, too, would have to accept existing and perhaps additional distortions. I think that is a fact of life of northwestern Ontario. If we wish to maintain the kind of presence we have been able to create in northern Ontario, we must accept these distortions and their consequences.
The last point 1 would like to make is that one of the factors which made it easy for us in northern Ontario to deal with this redistribution was that the Commission in Ontario published reasons for its decisions. There is a section in the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act that calls upon Commissions to publish the reasons in their reports upon which they make their decisions. That was the result of a Private Members' Bill that was sponsored by myself and the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) which we were successful in having passed.
This is really the first redistribution in which the Commission for Ontario has taken those recommendations seriously. If one goes over the report that it made, one can find that in each case for each region and many ridings individually reasons are given for the particulary selection of boundaries as well as justification of their decisions.
I have had an opportunity to review the action of Commissions in other Provinces and quite frankly their performance has been spotty indeed, to put it mildly. Many of them have put in the minimum possible to conform with the law, which leads me to believe that decisions in those cases were arbitrary, irrational and indefensible because the Commissions could not be bothered to put the reasons for these decisions in place.
It strikes me that one of the good things about the Ontario Commission and something that leads us in northern Ontario by and large to accept the results of the Commission is the fact that it published in detail-more detail than any other Commission-the reasons it had taken certain decisions. This
meant that when we came to appeal certain aspects of its decisions, we had all the data that was required to be able to do that. We were able to have arguments and discussions with the Commission that made sense as a result. Therefore, 1 want to commend the Ontario Commission for what it has done in general and I want to join with the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) and the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior in supporting the over-all directions it has given us in northern Ontario.

When it comes to Crown agencies and to the experience we have had in this House over the past number of years, even the Secretary of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) is on the public record as saying that he believes accountability of any expenditures of taxpayers' money must return to the Parliament. Also, that the Parliament of Canada must be able to scrutinize on behalf of the taxpayers the loans and operations of Crown Corporations and Crown agencies.
Let us take a look at the experience we have had over the past few years. In 1982-1983, we see that Canadair, a Crown corporation, lost some $1.4 billion; de Havilland lost $265.2 million; and VIA Rail lost $449 million in 1982. The estimated loss for VIA Rail for 1983-1984 is a horrendous $755 million. These are the taxpayers' concerns with regard to the accountability of Crown agencies in the expenditure of their money. It is not our money, Mr. Speaker, it is not the Government's money, it is the money belonging to the taxpayers of Canada. We can look at Canadian National which had an exceptionally poor year and lost money. Air Canada should not be compared with the other Crown agencies I have mentioned because for the first time in six years it has experienced a loss in its operations.
Let us come to one Crown agency that most Canadians deal with and are familiar with. I am speaking of Canada Post, which lost about $300 million. Taxpayers of Canada are saying, they are reiterating it to us as their Members of Parliament-and I am sure they are mentioning it to Members on the Government side-that there has to be some form, some way, some method of making these bodies more accountable for the expenditures of taxpayers' money. The people deemed to be entrusted with this responsibility must justify
September 16, 1983

their actions to the House of Commons or to the Parliament of Canada.
Legislation says that Crown corporations must file reports within three months of the end of their fiscal year. Let us look again at Canada Post. It is perhaps not a good example but it is an example which the people of Canada understand and deal with daily. Canada Post is now some 14 months overdue in the filing of its annual report.
We have heard during this debate that the Canadian Export Development Corporation will be called before a standing committee of the House of Commons and in that way will have to justify last year's operations. If we have legislation which allows Crown corporations to delay the filing of their annual reports for some 14 months, certainly the scrutiny of their books would be considered to be after the fact. There is not much that I or any other Member of Parliament could do in "after the fact" scrutiny when they are 14 months out of date. Approximately 65 per cent of Crown corporations or agencies do not meet the three-month deadline for filing annual reports at the close of the fiscal year.
In the consideration of this Bill there has been much discussion about the implementation and establishment of a similar organization under the direction of another Minister, namely Canagrex. The only difference between the establishment of Canagrex and that of the Export Development Corporation is Clause 29(4) of Bill C-85 which gave birth to Canagrex. It reads:
The accounts of Canagrex shall be audited annually by the Auditor General of Canada and the Auditor General may, where he deems it necessary, conduct a comprehensive audit of the affairs of the Corporation.
We see that as a step in the right direction. My understanding is that there is certainly a difference between a comprehensive audit and a general audit, as is the case with the EDC. A comprehensive audit provides the ability to go into the deep and internal operations of each department, the expenditures made and the ability to point out almost daily operations, either corrections or adjustments, whereas general audits are basically the balancing of numbers, taking a look at audit sheets and saying that the numbers are correct as they appear.
With the sad experience which Canadians have had, 1 do not suppose the Export Development Corporation is one that comes to mind. As we all know there are a great number of Crown corporations, some 300 of them. This does not necessarily bother me or Hon. Members on this side of the House. There is a great deal of employment in Crown corporations. Some 263,000 people are employed in such corporations. But in looking at the operations of Crown corporations, according to the 1982 report under the section entitled, "Matters of Special Importance and Interest", the Auditor General indicated:
Yet, in the aggregate, they represent a hole in the taxpayer's pocket, resulting, as they often do, in a consistent negative return on investment.
While I know that the Auditor General is not talking about the Export Development Corporation and that that corpora-
Export Development Act
tion does not enter into the same area as many agencies to which he referred, it must be incumbent upon those of us who are entrusted with the care of taxpayers' dollars, which they work very hard to earn, to have the ability to bring in a check, to bring to question and then change the activities of any Crown agency that is requesting, as is the EDC, a very substantial increase in its borrowing ability.
That borrowing ability amounts to a huge borrowing bill. For example, my Province of Saskatchewan has a $2 billion plus budget. Under the proposed Bill to reorganize the Export Development Corporation, there is included a borrowing ability which could be from $40 billion to as high as $60 billion. There is no recourse in the legislation to bring before Members of Parliament any accounting, with the exception, in fairness, of the annual report. If we go over annual reports of the past, as I have mentioned, we are lead to say that as much as we on this side recognize the value of trade and the energy and ability of the people involved in the EDC, to counterbalance and justify our existence here there must be some way of holding the corporation responsible to the Parliament of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot tell you how delighted I am to be here and to be able to speak to the House for a few moments today.

speechtext:
It is a pleasure to follow my good friend, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), whose speech I listened to with great interest, and at the same time to see the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) in the House to hear his Bill debated. It is becoming almost a precedent when the Minister responsible stays in the House for a debate, particularly on a Friday afternoon. I think he should be commended for being here. Also I am pleased to see the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) in the chair. We serve together on the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, and what I will say in the few minutes I have relates to the work of that committee and the issue of accountability.
I wanted to say those things at the outset because the Minister should understand that there is no objection from this Party, indeed from any Party, to any reasonable effort made by the Minister of State, the Ministry, any of his officials or any Crown corporation to increase trade. It is a trite to say about our country that trade is its lifeblood, but without it the country would wither and our standard of living fall; we would not enjoy the quality of life we have come to expect. It is not that quality with which 1 am dealing. The amendments deal with a matter of importance which is equally coming to the fore in terms of the operation of this place, the role of Hon. Members on all sides of the House of Commons and their place in the scheme of government-that issue is accountability-

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act
The Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) spoke yesterday in the debate. As reported at page 27157 of Hansard he
said:
-the question that is before the House today in this amendment is whether or not the amount of money requested, $20 billion, which would increase the borrowing capacity of the Export Development Corporation, is being requested and scrutinized in the proper manner.
That is the issue. For 18 months I have had the privilege of serving with other Hon. Members on the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure of the House of Commons, the parliamentary reform committee. We have concluded- and I draw this particularly to the attention of the House and the Minister-the seventh report of that committee, entitled the Huntington-Lachance report, the report of a Conservative and a Liberal both of whom directed and guided the committee to its unanimous conclusion that with respect to Government accounting generally and with respect to Crown corporation accounting particularly, it was hopelessly inadequate and something had to be done. The purpose of this amendment concerns in the context of Bill C-l 10, an objection to this lack of accountability.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read from that signal report, the seventh report of the special committee which deals with this issue. I am reading as follows from Paragraph 3 of the seventh report:
Your Committee feels that "accountability" is fundamentally important in a parliamentary democracy. The Committee is united in its commitment to establish a better system to permit the House of Commons to exercise greater influence in the examination of public expenditures and finance. The mechanisms we propose will permit the House of Commons and its committees to exercise new influence on the business of government. It is important to stress that this Committee is seeking for Parliament an increased influence-
And influence is underlined-
-in the analysis of governmental policies, not direct control of the Government.
Parliament is not the executive nor is the executive Parliament but there is an influence which Parliament should bring to bear. Continuing on, I quote:
The Committee fully accepts that the Executive must be free to make its judgments and to govern, subject of course to maintaining the confidence of the House of Commons.
That was the broad statement made with respect to that. As a result of that, the committee has proposed the establishment of a government corporations and agencies committee among others.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster mentioned that there are well over 300 Crown corporations. Some of them are Crown corporations as we understand them to be, some are Crown corporations created by Crown corporations, some are Crown agencies and some are subagencies. God knows that they proliferate, although Parliament does not know nor does the Government. This lack of accountability is something the Canadian people simply will not tolerate.
It is not that Crown agencies per se are bad. Some of them are quite necessary, but we are hopelessly at sea on the question of accountability, and something must be done about
it. Accountability must be given back to this institution which is the only institution to which the public has some input, however indirect, with respect to the accountability of the instruments of government.
We on that committee learned about how these agencies had been created and we were struck by the fact that a serious gap occurred because not all Crown corporations, not even those as defined in the Financial Administration Act, table annual reports that are made the subject of the mandate of the Auditor General. The system is clearly one that developed early on and is now inadequate.
As the influence of government moves through Crown agencies and departments the likes of which I have described, it becomes absolutely essential that each agency and department be made subject to the concept of accountability to Parliament, a concept which was basic to the establishment of Parliament in the first place.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I support the amendments we are dealing with, amendments 3 and 5, and that is why I believe the Government ought to think twice about what it is asking Parliament to approve for a corporation which has generally carried on a good and essential service in the operation of the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be afforded the opportunity to speak today on the amendments to Bill C-l 10 as proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), because I believe that what we are debating today goes to the very core of the responsibility of every Member of Parliament.
We as elected representatives of the country are empowered with the responsibility of protecting the public purse by ensuring that safeguards and controls are put in place for Parliament to be accountable to the taxpayers for the spending of every one of their dollars. I take that responsibility very seriously, as I am sure does every Member in this Chamber.
The mandate of the Export Development Corporation is to facilitate and develop Canada's export trade by providing insurance, guarantee and loan facilities. I am sure there is no Member in this Chamber who would argue with the fact that trade is of the greatest importance to the country. We are a nation that should exploit its trade possibilities to the limit. We produce goods and services beyond those which we as a nation can use ourselves, and it is therefore vitally important to our economy that we seek out those markets for export purposes.
The fundamental purpose of the Export Development Corporation is to assist our manufacturers to seek new customers on the international marketplace and to ensure and guarantee that the exporter will receive payments for these sales. These manufacturers must be protected from non-payment by foreign purchasers who may be unable to pay for their imports due to internal economic and political strife in their own countries and, of course, many other economic fluctuations.
September 16, 1983

2721 1
Our manufacturers must also be able to compete with other countries to enable them to take advantage of that export market. The corporation, through its loan guarantees at lower interest rates, enables more competitive offers to be made.
As 1 have stated, the matter of developing our export market is not the concern that is before us today. 1 am concerned with the efficiency with which the corporation functions and, more important, the accountability to Parliament for the corporation's expenditures, its operation and its administration.
The Export Development Corporation was described by Professor Andre Raynauld of the University of Montreal as "rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient". There is a great deal of merit to that statement when one looks at the number of employees employed by the corporation. EDC employs over 613 people, almost ten employees for each separate loan customer or one and a half employees for each insurance account. With statistics of that kind, I would question the productivity of the corporation and indeed the efficiency of its administration.
1 turn now to the amendments that are before us today. These amendments were introduced for the purpose of bridging the gap created by some glaring inadequacies of accountability that are present in this Bill and to effect some measure of parliamentary control over a Crown corporation.
We have seen, time and time again, blatant examples of Crown corporations administering taxpayers' money at their own will without the discipline of good, sound management, while incurring huge losses and plunging the country deeper and deeper into debt. The scandalous situation surrounding Canadair, which has incurred losses of some $1.4 billion, is a prime example of how some Crown corporations are mismanaging the taxpayers' dollars that come from what is thought of as a bottomless trough, the public purse.
I believe it is absolutely imperative that we bring back to Parliament effective control over the public purse. We must work toward this goal at every possible opportunity.
The amendments that we are debating today, if they were to be adopted by Parliament, as I would urge that the House do, would indeed prove to the Canadian people that we as Parliamentarians are putting into place those safety nets that will ensure a certain degree of control over taxpayers' money.
As I understand it, Bill C-110 is a request for approval of, among other things, the increase of capital authority to the Export Development Corporation from $1 billion to $2 billion. This would give the EDC the authority to borrow up to ten times against that capital authority. That would give it the authority to borrow $20 billion. That is $20 billion worth of borrowing authority which is beyond the control of Parliament and is on the credit of Canada. In other words, the Export Development Corporation will have the authority to borrow huge sums of money without ever having to come to Parliament for approval and without being accountable to the Par-
Export Development Act
liament of Canada for the administration of the spending of those funds. I find that totally unacceptable.
Slowly but surely through legislation of this kind, we are seeing the erosion of Parliament's control over Crown corporations. If this Bill is allowed to proceed in its present form without the adoption of these amendments, we will see the further erosion of Parliament's control over Crown corporations and their ability to spend tax dollars without being accountable.
It is essential, in my view, that Parliamentarians recognize this problem and bring it to the attention of the Government at every possible opportunity, in every possible way. I value most deeply the responsibility placed in me as a Member of Parliament by the electorate, to ensure that their interests are well served, and unless there is that accountability to Parliament, I as a Member of Parliament am not fulfilling my responsibility and duty to the constituents of my riding.
The Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability stated:
Accountability is the fundamental prerequisite for preventing the abuse of delegated power and for ensuring instead, that power is directed toward the achievement of broadly accepted national goals with the greatest possible degree of efficiency, effectiveness, probity, and prudence.
I believe most strongly that there is a need for effective legislation that will allow scrutiny and control over the expenditure of public funds, which is something we do not have with any degree of adequacy at present.
A poll taken recently showed that 64.6 per cent of the general public had little or no interest in the work of the House of Commons, which I find most unfortunate, and it is something which saddens me deeply. I believe that to a great extent, this indifference, this apathy toward Parliament, displayed by the majority of the Canadian people, comes from their loss of confidence in the Government and in the parliamentary system.
The taxpayers of Canada no longer feel that they are getting value for their dollar, and indeed why should they? There have been many, many examples of Parliament's losing control over the constant growth of its size and its expenditures. It is up to us, as Parliamentarians to demonstrate to the Canadian people that we are desserving of the trust placed in us by the electorate; that we demand that Parliament have ultimate and absolute control over expenditures and that Government departments and Crown corporations be accountable to Parliament for all their activities.
I believe it is time for these Crown corporations to be accountable to their shareholders, the taxpayers of Canada, for efficient management of their administration and appropriated funds.
The amendments that are proposed to Bill C-110 are the first steps toward bringing back some degree of accountability to the Parliament of Canada. 1 would urge all Members to vote in favour of these amendments.

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act

Mr. Speaker, I deeply oppose this Bill and support the amendments. Two issues are involved: one is responsible management and the other is accountability to Parliament. We have heard many Members on this side of the House articulate their position on these matters.
In fairness, however, I want to make it clear that my criticism is not criticism of the Export Development Corporation. In my community the relationship between a large company, Babcock and Wilcox Industries Limited, which employs a great number of people and this Crown corporation has been a good one. In Cambridge, where at a certain point in time unemployment was well over 20 per cent and where Badcock used to employ some 2,000 people, now, because of the recession and Government policies and serious mismanagement, this company employs under 1,000 people. The domestic market for Babcock products has shrunk to almost zero.
From the perspective of my community it is very, very important that sales be significant, particularly those of Babcock and Wilcox in our community, so that people can be employed.
I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from a letter written to me by the President of that company. They read:
Our major competition is from companies such as Mitsubishi in Japan, Combustion Engineering in the Untied States, and Babcock Power of the United Kingdom. These companies have spent a great number of years systematically developing markets throughout the world. One of the key parameters in this development has been financing, particularly government supported financing from Japan and the U.K.
On a large capital project, the financing can be more important than the products, many of which may be evaluated relatively equal by the customer. Our competition has realized this and has worked heavily with their governments to provide the type of financing necessary. The result has been impressive. The co-operation between EDC and B&W has been key to the level of success achieved so far in the much publicized Dendro project in the Philippines.

Let me say at the beginning that the magnitude of the borrowing in the amount of $20 billion is so staggering that it almost defies one's ability to comprehend such an exceedingly large sum of money. Surely the onus has to be on the Government to justify its need for such a prodigious sum of money as $20 billion.
The EDC is what is classified as a Crown corporation D. It is my understanding that the further down the alphabet a corporation comes-and I think they go to D-the more commercially viable they must be. In other words, the expectation is not that they are an instrument, necessarily, of public

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join today with my colleagues to debate Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, to speak against the Government and bureaucratic excesses which this Bill in its present form will allow, and to speak in favour of the reasonable and sensible amendments put forth by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).
As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, the Export Development Corporation was originally organized to ensure export transactions. This is very worthy, in other words, to provide Canadian producers with credit insurance, insuring the credit worthiness of their foreign purchases and sales, and to protect the producers against problems of non-payment from foreign countries because of political interference and so on. Of course, all of this we applaud.
As well, Mr. Speaker, the corporation's business is to become a lender, perhaps even a lender of last resort, certainly an important lender of moneys to expedite the sale of Canadian goods in foreign markets. That is the Export Development Corporation's necessary mandate, but it is even today a mandate which carries with it very little accountability to Parliament and to the taxpayers of Canada.
What the Government proposes to do with this Bill is to make the EDC even more unaccountable to Parliament. One would hope and expect that an agency which is charged with the disbursement of huge sums of money to be an effective and efficiently run body. Let us look briefly at the management of the corporation to see if that is so. The facts raise serious questions as to the efficiency of the corporation because there are at present some 613 employees of the Export Development Corporation. Last year, in 1982, the corporation dealt in loan accounts with 62 exports. This represents one customer for every ten employees.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is ridiculous.
Export Development Act

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
What bank does anyone know of which has ten employees per customer? Do Canadian taxpayers not have a right to an explanation of and correction of such waste of their dollars? The corporation, as I have previously pointed out, is involved with insurance. It had slightly in excess of 900 separate insurance policies placed during 1982. That is approximately one and one half insurance policies per employee. And we talk about productivity! In many senses this corporation is bureaucracy gone wild, and from that point of view alone should it be carefully examined. In these difficult times Canadian taxpayers cannot-and I suggest will not

afford such extravagance. These facts alone should cause the Minister to be seriously concerned with the efficiency of the operation of this Crown corporation.
How can a corporation which has transactions with but 62 companies justify offices-elegant offices-in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax, together with a head office here in Ottawa? Does nobody in the Government care about taxpayers' dollars? Parliament should be seeking more control of bureaucratic waste, not less control. Liberal Members should be demanding that the Cabinet exercise more control over waste and inefficiency, not sitting back while billions more taxpayers' dollars are assigned to this huge tax dollar gobbling machine. But no, Parliament will have even less control than it does today if this Bill passes.
Let us look at one part of the present Act which clearly illustrates how we, as Parliamentarians, have literally no cont-trol over the actions of the corporation. 1 will refer to Section 31 which reads:
Where the Minister reports to the Governor in Council that
(a)	the Board is of the opinion that a proposed loan or guarantee of the kind described in section 29 would, if made or issued, be for a term or in an amount of excess of that which the Corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one export transaction . . . and
(b)	in the opinion of the Minister it is in the national interest that the proposed loan be made or guarantee issued,
the Governor in Council may authorize the Corporation to make the proposed loan or give the proposed guarantee, as the case may be.
Effectively, loans of this nature can be made by the corporation up to $2.5 billion, and all that is necessary is an Order in Council, even if the corporation's executive itself decided the loan was not worthy. Obviously, Parliament is not necessary in this kind of an arrangement. The present arrangement whereby the Government of Canada can decide to take on export transactions by Order in Council, to take huge sums of money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, put the matter through as an advance without any parliamentary debate or question, is just incomprehensible. This type of arrangement and back room government must be stopped and not expanded.
Under Section 32 of the Export Development Corporation Act, as mentioned, the limitation of the Government to enter into Section 31 type transactions is $2.5 billion, as I have noted. The Government's effort in Bill C-l 10 is to increase this allowable amount for Cabinet generosities of dubious or questionable transactions to $10 billion. Remember, this $10 billion would be for the backroom boys in Cabinet to give out loans which the EDC itself had decided were bad risks. Can

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act
you believe that, Mr. Speaker? In effect, the Canadian people could be involved in more Algerian muniment deals, or Russian pipeline deals, as the Government may wish, to the extent of $10 billion without an aye, yes or no by any vote, by any Parliament, at any time. We on this side of the House cannot accept this section. No Member of Parliament should vote for this type of approval of borrowing and advancing vast sums of money with no strings attached.
Let us for a moment, Mr. Speaker, look at the concept of subscribed capital, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), pointed out a moment ago. Normally a trust company, loan company or bank is entitled to lend a multiple of its subscribed capital and earned surplus. In other words, if it has a million dollars in capital it may be permitted to issue some multiple of that amount, say, $10 million. The Export Development Corporation does not have that type of limitation. Its limitation, Mr. Speaker, is a multiple of authorized capital. In other words, the Government need not put up the money, as private lending companies must; it only has to say it has the capital. The effect of Bill C-l 10 is to increase the authorized capital to $2 billion, and the consequence of this maneuvering is that the authorized borrowing has increased to $20 billion. There is no requirement for the Government to subscribe for capital stock in the corporation. The subscriptions are meaningless. The borrowing limit now is to be $20 billion.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, what I am saying is that the way this Bill stands, the Government can spend $20 billion through the EDC without as much as a single word from Parliament, in effect giving the people of Canada no say in the spending of $20 billion of their hard-earned tax dollars.
The people of Canada expect their elected Members to oppose the hidden spending granted by this Bill and I urge all Hon. Members to do so when the vote occurs.

The hard, cold facts are that the EDC has never had a money-losing year in its entire operation. That is a matter of great laughter for the Hon. Member. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) compared it with the U.S. Exim Bank and spoke of how their method of lending money was preferable. I want to point out that that bank has to have conditional approvals in many instances, and that is a system under which exporters cannot efficiently operate. They never know if the loan is going to be approved. It is a substantial disadvantage. I also want to point out that statistics comparing the size of the United States with the size of Canada and the amount of their loans are not realistic because of the fact that this country is much more dependent upon sales abroad than is the United States. There is no country amongst industrialized countries more dependent on trade than Canada. We count on our exports for more than 31 per cent of our Gross National Product. We would not be able to have the standard of living that we have if we did not have the exports we have.
Some people have also been critical of the number of clients of the EDC and the fact that they are small in number and all of the loans are made to a relatively small number of organizations. What is not taken into account-and an Hon. Member referred to Babcock and Wilcox-is that many of those loans affect the sales of a great number of sub-contractors, as often happens with a company like Babcock and Wilcox. That is
September 16, 1983

why we are hearing from the exporters of this country, because a great number of them are affected, not just a few. It is also often the case that a consortium is involved.
Here we have a system which has worked well for ten years, Mr. Speaker. Why do these tinkerers always want to change something that is working well? I believe that if something works well you leave it. Here is a Crown corporation which has never had a loss, which is well run, which is servicing the exporters of this country in a way that pleases them, and it has to come here because it is nearing its loan limit and also to expand the board so that, as Hon. Members opposite desire, there can be more members from the private sector.
Today we found the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) using up the time of the House, instead of letting this Bill go through, in talking about the makeup of the board and the number of private members on the board and wondering why we did not codify it. He did not even read the Hansard record of the debates of two days ago or he would have heard exactly the position we have taken, that we guarantee to provide more private members, indeed a majority, but we are not prepared to codify the division between private and public sectors on any Crown corporation because that would not be a useful thing to do. It would be useful if Hon. Members at least prepared themselves by doing their homework before deciding to hold up the Bill further.

He also said there should never be such a thing as a Government account loan, with which I disagree. He referred to what he considered a horror, the Algerian monument deal. The Hon. Export Development Act
