subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Minister's non-political remarks. I must say that they raised a few questions in my mind. I heard him speak of the profit the Export Development Corporation had made, and it was as large as $2 million in one year, he told the House. However, he did not tell the House what the profits should have been relative to the investment of the Government in the corporation. I worked out the return on investment to be less than half of one per cent. That, for an investment on the part of a Government which pays 12 per cent to 16 per cent or whatever per cent interest on its debt, is a shocking performance. It is just incredible, and no person in business could ever exist with that kind of performance.
The Minister also told the House that the corporation was close to the end of its borrowing authority now, whereas the EDC, with borrowing authority of $10 billion, as of the end of the last fiscal year had used less than half, leaving it with $5 billion in the kitty still to use, and of its currently authorized $2.5 billion Governor-in-Council advances, only $700 million has currently been used.
In rising to discuss Motions Nos. 3 and 5 1 wanted to illustrate the importance of the debate and the importance of the financing of Crown corporations in general. These two amendments are proposing to cut back the Government's proposal in Bill C-110 for borrowing authority because they want a multiplier of ten times the share capital authorized. That would be $20 billion instead of the current $10 billion. The amendment is proposing to cut it back to a slight increase over the present $10 billion borrowing authority. The other amendment concerns the authorized capital, which could be any amount. It is the amount of capital that one can raise and

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act
spend that is the important feature. Therefore, this perfectly reasonable amendment in Motion No. 5 proposes to cut the borrowing authority back to ten times the aggregate of the paid-in capital and earned surplus, a much more reasonable figure.
Let us consider this situation involving Crown corporations for a moment. The particular corporation under discussion, the EDC, is one of 23 Crown corporations known as proprietary Crown corporations and listed in Schedule D of the Financial Administration Act. That is a reasonable number, but these 23 corporations have been rather prolific and have amongst themselves 114 subsidiary companies and 58 associated corporations. Altogether, the Government has identified 306 Crown corporations which employ some 263,000 people and which had assets, at the end of the last fiscal period, March 31, 1982, of $74 billion and liabilities of $63 billion. The Crown corporations are already $63 billion in debt, and in this one Bill the Government proposes to increase the total borrowing authority of one Crown corporation by $35 billion.
The Crown corporations themselves, at $63 billion, owed as much as the total budgetary estimates for the whole Government of Canada for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1982- an incredible amount. The amendments we are discussing today propose to control the amounts of these borrowings.
The Bill proposes a total increase of the borrowing authority of the EDC from $27 billion to $62 billion, an increase of $35 billion. The Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) explained that $1 billion or $10 billion was a large amount. 1 will give an example which 1 usually do not use in this Chamber to describe exactly what $1 billion is because today we are discussing a total of $35 billion in extra borrowing authority. If one had commenced on day one of the year zero A.D., in the first year of our Lord, with $1 billion and had started spending it at the rate of $1,000 a day, or $365,000 a year, an income exceeding that of most people we know, 1 am sure, such individual would today, on September 16, 1983, have over a quarter of a billion dollars left to spend, $276,311,000. That would be the amount left, after 1,983 years, of $1 billion only. Here we are discussing $10 billion.
This problem of the Crown corporations is not a new one. I know Your Honour has studied the problems of Crown corporations at some length when you were a member of the Public Accounts Committee. Over the past seven years, I can tell the House that there have been many attempts to study, control and improve the accountability of Crown corporations. The Auditor General has mentioned this in many of his reports, the Government itself has conducted studies and commissions have dealt with Crown corporations. Many reports of the Public Accounts Committee have commented and made recommendations on handling and accountability of Crown corporations. There have been Bills introduced into Parliament, Today, we might ask ourselves where all of that has brought us. The progress was so feeble that the Auditor General was moved in his last report to make three pertinent recommendations, which I would like to read into the record as follows:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
I have already referred to the enormity of the dollars involved with these corporations.
Another recommendation in the current report of the Auditor General is as follows:
Broad legislation for the accountability of Crown-owned corporations should be developed that will include provisions relating to each of the elements of authorizing and mandate, financing, directing, controlling and reporting. Such legislation should provide that these corporations be subject to comprehensive audits.
That is a very interesting subject. The other current recommendation on the same subject is as follows:
Parliament should give attention to issues surrounding control and accountability of those mixed enterprises and other entities and associates in which the Crown is a shareholder.
I want to make it clear that my comments in the debate are not in any way to be construed as a criticism of the EDC itself. The Auditor General himself had kind words for the EDC. it is one of the better run Crown corporations. To its credit, the executives of EDC appeared before the Public Accounts Committee on the subject of comprehensive audits. The EDC is an example of one of the good corporations that accepted and enjoyed a comprehensive audit. It was prepared to come and tell the committee and other Crown corporations what benefits were available to them if they agreed to a comprehensive audit.
The danger is that some Crown corporations will become instruments of Government policy rather than being allowed to run as they are. Because the amount of credit being proposed for this Crown corporation is as large as it is, that danger is multiplied many times, if the Crown corporation that becomes an instrument of public policy is successful, the Government will take credit for its success. But when things go badly, such as in the recent example of Canadair, the Government is all too ready to blame the civil servants, the executives or management of the corporation, or something else, such as the Opposition, the weather, or whatever comes into its mind. While the reports on the Canadair issue are not yet forthcoming from the Public Accounts Committee, it is my own presently held view that the Government is trying to make the management in that case the scapegoat and take the heat off what was obviously a determined Government policy. I see you rising, Mr. Speaker, and I will end my remarks now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few words to this debate. As we know, the amendments with which we are dealing are motions No. 3 and 5 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn). These amendments should be allowed to pass and be added to the Bill.
September 16, 1983

I listened very carefully to some of the Minister's remarks and I found his attitude rather strange. 1 might say that 1 have a high regard for the EDC and the people who run it, and that is what concerns us. My concern, and I think that of many of my colleagues, is that we do not trust the Minister and the Cabinet with what they are trying to do to EDC. When we look back upon some of the other fiascoes we have seen in Crown corporations and some of the messes which have been created by Consolidated Computer, Canadair and others, we are concerned that this not happen to EDC. That is the reason for my colleague's amendment, which seeks to codify the number of directors from the private sector who should be on the board of directors of EDC. We simply do not trust what the Government will do, and that is the basic problem. The Government could indicate that there will be a predominance of directors from the private sector in the first year and then change it all around in the next year in order to suit its own purposes. That is how devious the Government is.
One statistic of EDC which concerns me is the small number of accounts which it handles. The Minister said that the 62 members of the private financing export club have a lot of spin-off work for subcontractors. While it is true that there is much subcontract work, and 1 can remember sitting on the Finance Committee several years ago when EDC would not handle anything under $1 million , I am amazed to find that it still has a very small select clientele with which it deals. I believe that is deplorable.
There are many small and medium sized corporations in this country which could be involved in the export business. In fact, the Government has suggested that the small and medium sized business sector is the engine with which to turn the economy around and employ some of the 1.5 million unemployed. What greater way to achieve this than by involving many of those companies in export financing? One needs only to talk to some of those small and medium sized companies to find out what results they had from discussion with EDC. It is a shock to find that it does not seem to be interested. 1 had a personal experience with this before 1 became involved in Parliament. I had an experience in an export venture. We called EDC, which said it would return the call. We called it again, but we never heard from it. We eventually arranged the whole deal with a merchant bank in London, England, over the telex. While we still made our sale we could not do it through the EDC. In the final analysis I discovered that EDC was not interested in the size of the deal we put together. It amounted to only a few hundred thousand dollars, which may be nothing to the EDC but a great deal to a small company. For that reason I want to see more directors and a greater diversification of directors from the private sector on the board of EDC.
I am somewhat shocked at the number of employees which it has for the number of its clients. In commercial terms the ratio of approximately 10 EDC employees for every client it handles is ridiculous. While I am aware that export work is specialized and needs specialized knowledge, I can say that there are many companies in the private sector which do just
Export Development Act
as technical work as EDC, looking into financing of export sales, but certainly do not have that employee-client ratio.
If we look at this in straight, crass commercial terms, the EDC today is employing about $741 million in its capital account. The Minister has said that it made $1.1 million in its operations last year. This is absurd when considered as a return on investment because any board of directors or management group in the private sector which employed $741 million in capital and had a return of $1.1 million would be thrown out of the doors at the next shareholders' meeting. The Minister said that the greatest thing about EDC is that it has not lost any money. 1 hope that it would not lose money with all the backing of the Government of Canada it has. We should realize that when it goes to the private money market to borrow money it borrows it at a preferred rate, which is a better rate than the private sector has because it has the covenant of the Government of Canada behind it.
One place where it earned its money last year was not on its operations but on the insurance that it sold. That insurance is five times the cost of comparable insurance in the private sector. In other words, if the company wants its financing it must buy its insurance. That is where the EDC made its money, and not on its operations.
Why did it not make money on its operations? I would like to see a complete analysis of the sales that it made and the deals that it has refinanced. How many times is a deal refinanced and still called an asset? I would like an answer to that question. While some people may make comparisons such as putting the capital account of EDC into the bank where it would receive 10 per cent and therefore make approximately $100 million by doing so and comparing that to the $1.1 million which EDC made, it is only part of the mumbo-jumbo which people who do not know business like to deal with. I prefer to deal with the real world. In this case I can sense another Canadair or Consolidated Computer deal, and any number of others we have seen as a result of this increase in capital.
1 am also concerned that control is being further removed from Parliament. Our only defence is to put in an amendment to urge that more private sector people be appointed to the board of directors and the vice-chairman of the board to be elected by the board preferably be someone from the private sector so we can have some kind of balance. I just do not trust the people in the public sector who are on a myriad of these Crown corporations with which we have all sorts of problems. I hope that we can convince the Minister to change this provision so at least we can keep whatever bit of sanity there is in the EDC.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising to speak for ten minutes on this clause dealing with the Export Development Corporation. I would point out that of all Parties in this House ours is most interested in the stimulation of trade. We want to see as little government intervention as possible. We want to see as much

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act
foreign trade as possible. In principle, we support this kind of measure in terms of promoting the solid progress of any kind of export development. What we object to is the kind of open ended financing which the Government wants for this corporation.
I repeat, in terms of concept, if there is a way in which we can stipulate foreign trade and help Canadian companies grow and let a government corporation like this be a facilitator of foreign trade for our Canadian companies that will provide jobs for Canadians, we are all for it. However, I think we could list examples where this concept has turned out to be the reverse, where it has hurt and cut out Canadian jobs rather than stimulating them.
1 listened with interest to what the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) said a few moments ago in defence of the Algerian monument deal consummated a few years ago. He said, "The Algerian monument deal was a fabulous success" quoting the Member sitting behind him from Montreal who is Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. It was a fabulous success, we heard. Let us assume, in terms of providing jobs for Canadians, that that project did that. It provided jobs for design engineers, for fabricators and so forth. But what was repugnant to Canadians at the time, and still is today, is that through Canadian Government financing, support financing, that deal went through at something like 9.5 per cent interest. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) is listening very carefully. I think he will agree with me that the deal went through at about 9.5 per cent interest at a time when Canadians were financing businesses and homes at rates ranging from 18 per cent to 24 per cent. If it was good for the Government of Algeria, why could we not provide financing for Canadians at the same rate? That is what was repugnant to Canadians. It was not the fact that a deal had been struck with Algeria. It was the kind of concession made to a foreign Government when there was no room for Canadians at the same time for a concession of that kind.
The Minister also objected to the fact that some Members would like to see an examination by Parliament as to the kinds of deals made with foreign Governments. 1 can understand his reservations. I do not think that Parliament should examine every precise detail. There should not be that kind of intervention.
Two years ago we discovered almost by accident that Canada helped to facilitate a deal with the Soviet Union selling partially refined uranium which, in turn, would complete the refining process and then sell it to other countries. Is that kind of facilitation in the best interests of our country? Should we sell uranium to the Soviet Union which in its process can then sub-trade that produce to the Federal Republic of Germany, to Argentina, to Italy or to some unfriendly countries? Is that in the best interests of Canada?
We had an example today in the House. One of the Members from Hamilton raised the issue of Lada cars. In Moscow, Lada cars sell for $12,000. In Canada they sell for $6,000.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Some of the NDP people drive them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Is that providing jobs for Canadians when an export corporation can help put together a deal whereby a foreign product can be dumped on the Canadian market at 50 per cent of the price tag of its sale in its own country and in the process cut out jobs in the steel industry and in the automobile industry? As my friend, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) said, the NDP Member who raised the subject ought to know that Members of his own Party are driving those cars. We wonder about that. That is why we have questions about that kind of activity. But what we object to most is the change in the role and the size of this corporation. It used to be a kind of insurance company so that Canadian companies dealing with a foreign company would have insurance in case a deal fell through after delivery had been made and payment was not forthcoming. Insurance would be there so the company would remain solvent and it would get its money.
Now, by the provisions in this legislation, that will be only a small appendage, only a small part of that business. As my friend, the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) mentioned, insurance happens to be the money-making side of the corporation, even though the interest of the corporation is now in financing. With good reason we can understand that the return on investment is only about one-half of 1 per cent.
The other objection we have is the size of the corporation. It is mushrooming out of all context to its previous role. It looks so innocent to see a provision in this clause which says this corporation wants to have an infusion of $2 billion. The general public may not understand that that $2 billion mushrooms to a total of effective financing of $62 billion. With $2 billion it extends by tenfold the borrowing authority of the corporation on its own. You already have $22 billion there. Then the Cabinet is allowed a $10 billion override above that. If the corporation decides there is a deal that is not in the best interests of the corporation but the Cabinet likes it, Cabinet can override the decisions of the corporation to the tune of $10 billion. Then the Cabinet can give an extra $10 billion in loan guarantees outside the purview of the decisions of this corporation. As well, there is $20 billion in insurance that can be added on top of that. What looks like a $2 billion infusion of capital is actually a $62 billion extravaganza now at the disposal of this corporation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: How much?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
This is why we object to the lack of parliamentary control over the activities of this corporation. The $2 billion we can perhaps understand. But the $62 billion is out of all reason. If the corporation wants to do business to the tune of $62 billion, we think it should have to come back to Parliament for approval at certain stages before it can spend that kind of money for insuring that kind of money. Therefore, we have introduced these amendments which would limit the amount the corporation can do, so that Canadian taxpayers will not be in a state of jeopardy as a result of the open-ended
September 16, 1983

financing which is now available to the Export Development Corporation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, various speakers for my Party commenting on this Bill have endeavoured to make it clear that we are very much in favour of increasing Canada's exports and export capability. We very much recognize that in the world of international trade today the utility of the Export Development Corporation or a corporation of that type to help in the financing of international transaction is very useful, in fact perhaps even essential given the competition from other countries. The fact that we are in favour of export financing and the fact that we recognize Canada must compete are insufficient reasons for the Government to ask us to set aside our responsibilities as Members of Parliament and the other considerations as responsible Parliamentarians that we should bear in mind and simply rubber-stamp what the Government is asking us to do. There is simply too much borrowing authority asked for in the Bill. Simply too much is being asked for, with no opportunity for Parliament to call to account, to discover or to exercise any sort of control over how the borrowing authority is utilized.
Whether we are talking about taking tax dollars from Canadian citizens and spending them or pledging the assets of Canadian citizens for a loan, the effect is exactly the same. There is no difference in substance. Yet for some reason one would get the impression that the Government thinks there is. 1 am sure it would never ask the House for $60 billion in cash taxing authority and say, "Never mind how it will be spent; just give us the $60 billion cash and we will spend it wisely". I do not think the people of Canada would tolerate that; the Government would not ask for it. But in essence that is exactly what is happening here.
Since 1 have been a Member of Parliament for the last 11 years, there has been a constant issue which started before I came, that is, the question of how we control Government spending. There has been a prevailing feeling substantiated by evidence and a concern expressed by responsible Canadians from all walks of life about the nature of Government spending and the controllability of Government spending. Over the last few years the portion of the Gross National Product being spent by Government continues to grow in spite of what are apparently the best efforts of Government to try to control it. We have had task forces, royal commissions and any number of investigations by Government agencies, non-Government agencies, private institutions and academics looking into the fundamental problem of how to control Government spending. The solutions have been varied. Some have been introduced by Government-the envelope system in Cabinet and so on. There has been a consistent theme from everyone who has proposed solutions, whether it be the Lambert Commission to which the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) referred earlier or the Glassco Commission, that there has to be openness about Government spending. The people have to know how much is being spent and how it is being spent. In other words, there has to be accountability to Parliament. That
Export Development Act
has been the fundamental bedrock. That in itself will not bring Government spending under control, but without it there is no hope of bringing Government spending under control. That has been the consistent theme of everyone who has looked at it.
This Bill is simply inconsistent with that consistent theme. This Bill indicates that we as Parliamentarians will delegate to this independent body the authority to spend $60 billion. We certainly will have no right to intervene in that spending, none whatsoever. We will not even be able to find out how it will be spent. I know, I have inquired of this particular corporation in the past about a number of transactions, only to be told, "I am sorry, these are commercial transactions and there is confidentiality involved because of the commercial nature of the transactions". Merely being a Member of Parliament, only having been elected by the citizens who are responsible for the money that corporation is spending, does not give me the right or ability to find out how it is being spent! No one shall know except themselves.
It is a source of frustration and indeed anger that so often we have a position or philosophy with which the Government agrees, such as the question of accountability, responsibility or openness about spending. I am sure no one on that side would say that be is in favour of keeping Government spending secret. No one would say that he is in favour of the public not knowing how its money is being spent. They would all insist that in fact the public should know and Parliament should know. I am sure that is the position of the Government. In spite of that position, it produces legislation like this saying, "But in this instance, so as to help trade and to give this corporation more money we want you to delegate your right to control the public purse and give this separate non-accountable group the authority to borrow and spend $60 billion". That is simply unsatisfactory. Also I would suggest that it is very shortsighted in terms of the Government's other responsibilities.
I have heard Ministers of Finance say to the House and to the public that the difficulties they had controlling the Canadian economy, influencing it or doing things about interest rates, unemployment and growth, were that the federal Government's direct spending as a portion of total Government spending had been decreased; that in fact the amount of spending through the Consolidated Revenue Fund which was not statutory and over which they had influence and the decisions they could make were relatively limited. A great deal of Government spending is established by statute. Their flexibility is very limited and, because of that limited flexibility, they are unable to exercise the kind of control and beneficial regulation of the economy which they might choose to do. If that is the case, why in blazes is the Government delegating to this separate group, over which it will have no day to day control, the authority to spend $60 billion? How can it rationalize the two positions? Yet we get that constantly. How can it justify this kind of Bill in the face of its decision not to proceed with the Crown Corporations Bill introduced in 1979 by the Clark Government which had in fact been written before that? How can the Government justify this extraordinary amount of

September 16, 1983
Export Development Act
money to this Crown corporation when we do not have legislation which allows the House to exercise the responsibility on behalf of taxpayers that taxpayers expect of us? One could perhaps forgive this legislation if it had been preceded by a Crown Corporations Bill that would provide that authority.
1 regret to see that you are rising, Mr. Speaker. 1 was just starting to clear my throat and get warmed up. Perhaps I will have another opportunity to speak.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to be able to speak on the amendments to the Bill to limit spending by this Crown corporation to $1 billion from $2 billion in terms of capital expenditure.
One of the problems that is faced by this country is the problem of debt. 1 believe that it is increasingly becoming a concern of the constituents of the country, and more particularly the taxpayers of the country, that spending, particularly by the Government we have had for the last 15 years, has gone out of control. It is interesting to note that when 1 came to the House in 1979, the total debt of the country was something like $78 billion. I am now given to understand that the total debt of the country is something like $160 billion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Are you responsible for that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
No, I am not responsible for that. That is a pretty dramatic increase in debt and 1 believe that that is what we are talking about in the type of amendment that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is endeavouring to put forward. We are endeavouring to control this type of exaggerated spending.
1 would first like to point out that in terms of the Export Development Corporation and international trade, our Party stands very positively in favour of getting into the export markets to create trade which would bring to the country a balance of payments that would be in the best interests of the country.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, 1 have had the pleasant experience of being appointed the critic for the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is a good example of a Crown corporation that has had a very positive effect on the country. In fact, export trade in wheat has brought a surplus to the balance of payments of the country of some $6 billion, with very direct credit, I believe, first to the producers of the country and also to a well run Crown corporation.
If that were to be the end of the story, it would be a very positive story. However, that is not the end of the story. There are some 306 Crown corporations in the country, the accumulated debt of which I understand is in excess of some $62 billion. 1 can say that the taxpayer is very concerned about the country's ever-escalating and accumulating debt. If this trend is to continue, we must ask ourselves what the outcome will be. Will it be a situation in which we give credit to those who do not need credit? 1 personally believe in charity. I am
all for it. I believe that there is a definite need for charity when we know that we are helping the starving.

But it begins at home, that is right. This Crown corporation happens to be one that has not used the full extent of the credit in its coffers. It is my understanding that there was some $500 million worth of credit available that was not used. Yet the Government is seeking an extension which goes even beyond the portion that was not used by the Crown corporation. Because of this, we must certainly strike a balance when seeking out new opportunities.
One would say that we stand only to criticize the direction taken by the Government. One would immediately ask what positive direction we would give to an export corporation and what kind of positive effect we feel it should have on the country. I am certain, and it looks very positive from a political standpoint, that within a few months, there could be a change of Government, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The direction that the country is taking could be changed from one of ever-increasing debt to one that is very, very positive. It will become very important that agencies such as the Export Development Corporation have a positive influence on primary producers, not only in the areas of agriculture, timber, mining and other resources but that it have a very positive effect on every area in which the primary producer is involved. 1 believe that that is our number one responsibility.
An Hon. Member who spoke earlier complimented the Export Development Corporation on the fine job that it has done. That is important, but it is also important to continue in a positive way, not in a way which will create even greater debt for the taxpayer. It is important to create a climate in which the primary producer can do his job and put his goods on the export market in a way that will have a positive effect upon the nation of Canada and a positive effect upon the primary producer. This is most important to the farmer, someone who is familiar with the hard work that goes into production at the primary level. I believe that it is very important to the producers that we have the responsibility for handling the funds that are so necessary.
In the past few years, we have seen an economic downturn. If there has ever been a time when it has been important to handle the finances of the country in a very delicate and concise way but in a way which is responsible, now is the time. We do not see from this Bill that the Government is doing that. We do not see that the Government is carrying out its responsibilities when calling for excess amounts of money to be used. There is a possibility of doubling the authorized capital of $1 billion and ten times that makes a total of $20 billion worth of taxpayers' money that could be used in extending credit, which would throw the country further into debt.
September 16, 1983

I believe that the time has come when we must take a very, very close look at the creation of debt that the Government has been involved in. We must turn that around and create a positive involvement in export sales, which will have the positive effect of building up the country and lessening the load on the taxpayer. We should build for the future of this great country and the generations that are to follow.
Let us look positively at the future, Mr. Speaker. Let us look forward in a way that would not enslave our taxpayers and put them further into debt so that when we come back here in five years, we will not be dealing with $200 billion as opposed to $160 billion but, rather, that we can look at the positive side of the sheet and say that Canada is strengthened economically, to the benefit of all its people.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate because we are dealing with what is, potentially, one of the most serious problems facing the country.
1 want to put it on record that there is not one Member of the Progressive Conservative Party who is not madly in love with the Export Development Corporation. We believe in it; we believe it helps Canadians with their exports, but we do not believe it should be abused in the way the Government proposes. It is an important institution which helps us compete in the export market.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, just because we believe it is a good and important institution does not mean that we should not criticize the attempt to administer different areas of the corporation in ways with which we disagree. We believe it has done an excellent job over the years and will probably do a better job in years to come-especially when this Party forms the Government, as we hope will be the case.
We should not abuse such important institutions or allow them to fall into disrepute because of the manner in which we manipulate them for the purposes of the Government-purposes, I might add, which the Canadian people are sick and tired of.
Let us consider one of the main reasons why the Progressive Conservative Party is so popular in the polls today and why the Liberal Government is so unpopular. It is because the people are sick and tired of the Government spending money which it does not have, and thus creating a larger and larger national debt. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not going to be around to pay it off, but his children will be. Fortunately, they are going to inherit a few million dollars, but the average Canadian realizes that his children are going to have to struggle. They should not be faced with even greater taxes imposed by future Governments in order to pay off mammoth debts created by the present Government because of its incompetent financial management.
That is the key thing to remember, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians are worried about the deficit and the unrestricted
Export Development Act
borrowings by this Government. The deficit this year will be $28 billion, give or take a few hundred million here and there.
Let us see what the Government is trying to achieve through this Bill and what the amendments would stop it from doing. At present the Export Development Corporation has paid up capital of $700 million and is entitled, under the present legislation, to borrow a total of $4.7 billion; right there it has $5.4 billion. Then there is insurance of about $2 billion. I am not sure at this date how much there is in guarantees but say about $2 billion. There is also the Government account; to cover instances when the Export Development Corporations says, "There is no way we want to touch that lemon" but the Cabinet says, "Oh, yes, this is politically desirable." That account is around $700 million, I believe. It ends up with commitments of around $10 billion.
Under the present legislation the Government has the right to continue to expand its borrowings up to approximately $27 billion, so we are $17 billion away from a complete ceiling. What would the Government's rights be as a result of the amendments? It wants to increase the paid up capital to $2 billion. At ten times that for loan purposes, it would end up with about $22 billion. It wants $10 billion set aside for the Cabinet to pass Orders in Council on its own account after the Export Development Corporation turns applications down but for political reasons the Cabinet thinks the corporation should let them go through. That brings it up to $32 billion. The Cabinet wants to have another $10 billion on top of that so that it can give loan guarantees to people like Maislin- perhaps not Maislin, but to various other organizations, for something that other bankers have turned down. That brings it up to $42 billion. Then it wants a $20 billion proviso for credit insurance. The total is about $62 billion, Mr. Speaker. It has now only used up to $10 billion of its allowance of $27 billion, so it is $17 billion short. However, it wants to increase its rights to $60 billion before it has even used up that other $17 billion.
When we consider that in the last 20 years it has used up $10 billion, we must ask if the Government is going to become completely crazy and spend all of the excess before it is kicked out of power. It has to call an election before February 18, 1985-18 or 19 months from now. Unless every Member of Cabinet proved to be a drunken sailor on a spending spree, it would be impossible to blow that amount of money in the time left to the Government.
The people of Canada do not trust the Government now because of the way it handles money. When it only has 19 months left to be in power, why should the people give it the right to give loan guarantees of $20 billion here, insurance guarantees there and to order things on its own account up to such a mammoth amount? Why does it not come back to Parliament every one or two or even three or four years to get approval for these things?
If we open this up to the amount of $62 billion that, along with the deficit and along with the other Crown corporations that are entitled to build up deficits, all of which comes back

on the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayer, then it is no wonder people are worrying about the future.
That has not happened yet. Canada is a country of great promise and it will have even greater promise when we get a new Government. In other countries which had promise, where Governments have gone berserk like Brazil, Jamaica, Turkey, Argentina or Mexico, the people are having to pay the price of governments borrowing more money than even optimism, hope or the good fortunes of those countries will make possible to be returned in future.
It is foolish for us to fall into that trap. Being cautious, we do not want to give a spendthrift Government the right to be more of a spendthrift. The Canadian public is very upset at the way the Government has spent the money and how it has increased the national debt in the time it has been in office.
We, as Members of Parliament, have a right to try to protect the public purse on behalf of taxpayers instead of giving the Government a blank cheque which would allow it to spend for years, even if it were to spend prudently.
We encourage the Export Development Corporation to seek parliamentary approval every second year or perhaps every third year. We would like to examine these matters in a much detailed manner.
I am sorry that my time has run out, Mr. Speaker, because there are many more matters for which I have great concern.
